```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
```
```{r}
#Part A
name <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli")
age <- c(20, 21, 19, 22, 20)
passed <- c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE)
students <- data.frame(name = name, age = age, passed = passed)
print(students)
print(typeof(students$name))
print(class(students$name))
courses <- data.frame(
course_code = c("IS101", "IS102", "IS103"), units = c(3, 3, 2), instructor  = c("Dr. P. Reyes", "Dr. R. Santos", "Dr. S. Cruz"))
print(courses)
```
1. A data frame is a rigid 2D grid where every column must have the same number of rows. Mismatched lengths break this structure, causing R to throw an error.
2. A data frame is a list of equal-length vectors under the hood, which allows each column to have its own data type (like text, numbers, or logicals) while keeping the overall table structure.
```{r}
#Part B
print(students$age)
print(students[["age"]])
print(students["age"])
print(class(students$age))
print(class(students[["age"]]))
print(class(students["age"]))
print(students[2, ])
print(students[3, "name"])
print(students[students$passed == TRUE, ])
print(students[students$passed == TRUE & students$age > 19, ])
```
3.Using single brackets [ ] keeps the data frame wrapper intact (returning a 1-column data frame), whereas $ extracts the column directly as a raw vector (returning its underlying data type, like "numeric").
4. Using & performs an element-wise "AND," returning TRUE only when both conditions are met simultaneously. Switching to | performs an "OR," returning TRUE if a student meets either condition (passing or being over 19).
```{r}
#Part C
str(students)
print(dim(students))
print(nrow(students))
print(ncol(students))
print(names(students))
summary(students)
```
5. summary() adapts to each data type: it calculates numeric statistics (min, quartiles, mean, max) for numeric columns, tallies TRUE/FALSE counts for logicals, and lists basic metadata (length, class, mode) for character strings where mathematical summaries don't apply.
6. str() is best for inspecting data structure (dimensions, column types, and sample values), while summary() is best for statistical overview (data ranges, distributions, and value counts).
```{r}
#Part D
students$year_level <- c(2, 3, 1, 4, 2)
print(students)
students$passed <- NULL
print(students)
print(students[order(students$age), ])
print(students[order(students$age, decreasing = TRUE), ])
```
7. Running students$passed == TRUE after dropping the passed column evaluates NULL == TRUE, returning an empty logical(0) vector. This fails to filter any rows and usually breaks subsequent code.
8. order(students$age) outputs the row indices sorted by age (e.g., c(3, 1, 5, 2, 4)). Passing these indices into the row slot of students[order(...), ] reorders the entire data frame row by row from youngest to oldest.
```{r}
#Part E
grades <- data.frame(name    = c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli"), midterm = c(85, 78, 92, 88, 70), final   = c(90, 82, 95, 84, 75))
grades$average <- (grades$midterm + grades$final) / 2
print(grades)
grades$remarks <- ifelse(grades$average >= 75, "Passed", "Failed")
print(grades[grades$remarks == "Failed", c("name", "average")])
print(grades)
```
9. grades$final - grades$midterm creates a change column (negative for drops, positive for gains), while a logical column like grades$midterm < 75 flags low scores. Sorting by these new columns immediately highlights struggling and improving students.
Conclusion
R data frames are list-based grids of equal-length vectors that preserve individual column data types. Use $ to extract raw vectors for filtering and [ ] to keep the tabular structure intact. Structural checks rely on str(), statistical overviews on summary(), and data manipulation on combining vector math, logical operators, and order().
